questions.q: What is the primary purpose of the "Before You Read" stage when approaching a non-fiction text like Shaw's "Freedom"?
questions.a: The primary purpose is to build a mental framework by researching the author's background, historical context, key vocabulary, and philosophical stance so that the reader can anticipate arguments, recognize bias, and comprehend complex ideas more easily. A wrong answer (e.g., "to summarize the essay" or "to answer the questions at the end") reveals the student confuses pre-reading with during-reading or post-reading tasks, missing that context activates prior knowledge and sets a purpose for reading.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why knowing that G.B. Shaw was a Fabian socialist helps you understand his essay "Freedom" better.
questions.a: Knowing Shaw was a Fabian socialist signals that he advocates gradual democratic reform rather than violent revolution, and that he views economic inequality as a systemic issue — not individual failure. This helps you interpret his distinction between "natural slavery to Nature" and "unnatural slavery to man" as a critique of capitalism, and his sarcasm about voting ("choose which of two rich friends will exploit you") as a Fabian critique of bourgeois democracy. A wrong answer (e.g., "it tells us he was a famous writer") shows the student treats biography as trivia rather than an interpretive key.

questions.q: Apply the pre-reading strategy to J. Krishnamurti's "Understanding Freedom and Discipline": List three specific things you would research about Krishnamurti before reading, and for each, state what insight it might give into his argument.
questions.a: 1. Research: Krishnamurti's rejection of the Theosophical Society's "World Teacher" role in 1929. Insight: Explains his insistence on "no guru, no authority" and why he equates discipline with conformity. 2. Research: His educational philosophy (e.g., Brockwood Park, Rishi Valley schools). Insight: Clarifies his focus on "tenderest age" and "sowing the seed of freedom" — he speaks from direct experience with students. 3. Research: The 1950s-60s context of post-independence India's education system. Insight: Reveals his critique of rote learning and "walls of do's and don'ts" as a response to colonial-era schooling. A wrong answer listing generic facts (birth/death dates, nationality) shows the student cannot distinguish relevant context from trivia.

questions.q: Analyze the difference in historical context between Shaw's "Freedom" (written 1930s) and Krishnamurti's talk (likely 1950s-60s). How might this difference shape their respective definitions of freedom?
questions.a: Shaw writes amid the Great Depression, rise of fascism/communism, and industrial capitalism — his freedom is socio-economic: leisure, fair wages, ending "wage slavery." Krishnamurti speaks in post-colonial India amid nation-building, where education was used for conformity — his freedom is psychological: freedom from conditioning, tradition, and fear. Shaw sees freedom as structural (laws, unions, distribution); Krishnamurti sees it as individual (inquiry, sensitivity, intelligence). A wrong answer that says "both talk about freedom so they mean the same thing" ignores how historical material conditions shape philosophical concepts.

questions.q: Evaluate this student's pre-reading note: "Shaw and Krishnamurti both hate discipline. Shaw says it's slavery; Krishnamurti says it's a prison. So they agree." Is this a valid synthesis? Justify.
questions.a: No, it's a superficial synthesis that conflates two distinct concepts. Shaw critiques *social* discipline (economic coercion, laws enforcing inequality) — he wants *just* laws and fair distribution. Krishnamurti critiques *psychological* discipline (conformity, imitation, authority) — he wants *no* external discipline, only self-awakened intelligence. Shaw accepts reasonable laws as increasing freedom; Krishnamurti sees all external discipline as contradictory to freedom. The student misses the socio-economic vs. psychological distinction — a classic "same word, different meaning" error.

questions.q: Create a 3-column "Context Comparison Table" for the two essays with these headers: Author & Identity | Historical Moment | Core Metaphor for Unfreedom. Fill it with precise, text-ready entries.
questions.a:
| Author & Identity | Historical Moment | Core Metaphor for Unfreedom |
|-------------------|-------------------|----------------------------|
| G.B. Shaw: Fabian socialist, playwright, critic; uses satire & irony | Interwar Britain (1930s): Depression, rise of totalitarianism, industrial capitalism | "Wage slavery" — the worker sells labour to a master who owns the means of production |
| J. Krishnamurti: Spiritual teacher, rejected guru status; emphasizes direct perception | Post-independence India (1950s-60s): Nation-building, formalized education, tradition vs modernity | "Prison walls of tradition" — the mind enclosed by authority, conditioning, and imitation |

A poor answer uses vague entries like "old times" or "society" — showing the student cannot extract specific, usable context from research.
